config.title: useCallback for Stable References

intro.title: useCallback for Stable References
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple counter app with a button that logs a message to the console. You will learn how to use the useCallback hook to create a stable function reference, preventing unnecessary re-renders of child components. The core concept is memoization, which helps optimize performance by caching functions. You will work with React hooks, functional components, and event handlers in a TypeScript environment. This is a beginner-friendly introduction to managing function dependencies in React.
intro.usecase: In Angular applications, maintaining stable function references is crucial for performance in interactive dashboards with dynamic filters. When users adjust multiple filter controls (date ranges, categories, or search terms), each change triggers re-renders of dependent components like data tables or charts. Without stable callback references, these components unnecessarily re-render even when their inputs haven't changed, causing lag in data-heavy interfaces. This pattern is essential for smooth user experiences in analytics platforms, admin panels, and real-time monitoring tools where filter interactions are frequent.

objectives: Implement useCallback to create stable function references in Angular components
Apply useCallback to optimize child component re-renders by preventing unnecessary prop changes
Configure useCallback dependencies to control when function references update
Integrate useCallback with event handlers to maintain consistent function identity
Manipulate component state using callback functions wrapped with useCallback
Construct performance-optimized components by combining useCallback with memoized child components
Update existing components by replacing inline functions with useCallback-wrapped functions

steps.title: Import Component, OnInit, and ChangeDetectorRef from Angular core
steps.instruction: Import Component, OnInit, and ChangeDetectorRef from '@angular/core'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import multiple symbols from the Angular core module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple Angular core modules
import { Component, OnInit } from '@angular/core';
steps.seedCode: // Import Component, OnInit, and ChangeDetectorRef from '@angular/core' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The Angular core modules needed for component creation and change detection are imported.
successCriteria: Component, OnInit, and ChangeDetectorRef are imported from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing all three symbols: Component, OnInit, and ChangeDetectorRef from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is incorrect. Please import Component, OnInit, and ChangeDetectorRef from '@angular/core' using the correct syntax.

steps.title: Create the main component class with OnInit implementation
steps.instruction: Create a component class named 'CallbackDemoComponent' that implements the OnInit interface. Use the @Component decorator with an empty selector and template for now.
steps.hint: Remember to use the 'implements' keyword and include the ngOnInit method.
steps.seedCode:
import { Component, OnInit, ChangeDetectorRef } from '@angular/core';

// Create the CallbackDemoComponent class here
steps.expectedOutcome: A component class named CallbackDemoComponent is created with proper TypeScript syntax implementing the OnInit interface.
successCriteria: Uses @Component decorator with selector and template properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your component class implements OnInit and includes the ngOnInit method.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created a class named CallbackDemoComponent that implements OnInit with the @Component decorator.

steps.title: Initialize component state with a counter value
steps.instruction: Inside the CallbackDemoComponent class, add a public property named 'count' with type 'number' and initialize it to 0.
steps.hint: Add 'count: number = 0;' as a property declaration in your component class.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a typed state property 'count' initialized to 0, ready to be used in the template and methods.
successCriteria: The component class contains a public property 'count' with type annotation 'number' and initial value 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a property named 'count' with the type 'number' and initialized it to 0. Check that it's properly typed and accessible within the class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't have the required state property. Add a public property named 'count' with type 'number' and initial value 0 inside the CallbackDemoComponent class.

steps.title: Create a regular function that increments the counter
steps.instruction: Inside the CallbackDemoComponent class, define a method named incrementCounter that increases the count property by 1.
steps.hint: Add a method to the component class that modifies the existing count property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a method that can be called to increment the counter, but this method will create a new reference each time it's accessed.
successCriteria: The incrementCounter method is defined in the component class and correctly increments the count property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a method, but it might not be incrementing the count property correctly. Make sure the method increases the count value by 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The incrementCounter method is not properly defined. Check that you've added a method to the component class that modifies the count property.

steps.title: Add ChangeDetectorRef dependency to the component
steps.instruction: In the constructor of your CallbackDemoComponent, inject ChangeDetectorRef as a private property to enable manual change detection control.
steps.hint: Use TypeScript's private modifier in the constructor parameter to automatically create and store the service instance.
steps.analogousExample:
// Injecting a service for manual control
constructor(private myService: MyService) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component constructor now has ChangeDetectorRef properly injected as a private dependency.
successCriteria: ChangeDetectorRef is injected in the constructor with the private cdr parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure ChangeDetectorRef is properly injected as a constructor parameter with the private modifier.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added ChangeDetectorRef as a private parameter in the constructor. The syntax should be: constructor(private cdr: ChangeDetectorRef) {}

steps.title: Create a stable callback using a class property with arrow function
steps.instruction: Add a class property called stableIncrement that is an arrow function which increments the count property and calls this.cdr.detectChanges() to trigger change detection.
steps.hint: Define the property directly in the class body using arrow function syntax to automatically bind 'this' context.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a stable callback function that increments the counter and triggers Angular's change detection.
successCriteria: The stableIncrement property is defined as an arrow function that increments count and calls this.cdr.detectChanges()
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the stableIncrement property, but make sure it increments the count and calls this.cdr.detectChanges() to properly update the UI.
steps.feedbackWrong: The stableIncrement property is missing or incorrectly defined. Remember to use arrow function syntax and include both the increment operation and change detection call.

steps.title: Set up the component template with basic structure
steps.instruction: Inside the @Component decorator's template property, add a container div with a heading that says 'Counter Demo'.
steps.hint: The template property should contain HTML. Use double quotes for the template string.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a basic HTML structure with a heading inside a container div.
successCriteria: The template property contains a div element with an h2 heading displaying 'Counter Demo'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some template content, but make sure it includes a div with an h2 heading that says 'Counter Demo'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template structure is missing or incorrect. Add a div element with an h2 heading containing the text 'Counter Demo'.

steps.title: Display the current counter value in the template
steps.instruction: Inside the component's template, add a paragraph element that displays the current value of the count property using interpolation.
steps.hint: Use double curly braces {{ }} to bind the count property value in the template.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will show the current count value when the component renders.
successCriteria: The template contains a paragraph element with interpolation that displays the count property value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a paragraph element with interpolation syntax {{ }} that references the count property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't yet display the count value. Add a paragraph element with interpolation to show the current count property value.

steps.title: Add buttons for both increment methods and wire their click events
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add two buttons: one that calls the incrementCounter() method and another that calls the stableIncrement() method when clicked.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (click)="methodName()" for each button.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will contain two buttons with click events bound to the component's increment methods.
successCriteria: Two buttons are present in the template, each with a (click) event binding to the correct method: one to incrementCounter() and one to stableIncrement().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added buttons, but make sure each button's (click) event is correctly bound to the corresponding method: one to incrementCounter() and one to stableIncrement().
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't contain the required buttons with click event bindings. Add two buttons with (click)="incrementCounter()" and (click)="stableIncrement()".

steps.title: Add visual indicators to show function reference stability
steps.instruction: In the component template, add two paragraph elements: one explaining that the 'Increment with Regular Method' button uses an unstable reference, and another explaining that the 'Increment with Stable Callback' button uses a stable reference.
steps.hint:
Add

tags inside the template with descriptive text about each button's function reference behavior.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will include two explanatory paragraphs that help users understand the difference between stable and unstable function references.
successCriteria: Two paragraph elements are added to the template with text explaining the reference stability of each button.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some text, but make sure you have two separate paragraph elements explaining both button behaviors.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't contain the required explanatory paragraphs about function reference stability.
